question: The Court of Justice of the European Union judgment in case C-330/211 confirmed that Member States may apply reduced value added tax (VAT) rates to the use of sporting facilities and certain ancillary coaching services. However, recent reforms in several Member States have led to many fitness, sport and leisure-activity services being subject to the full VAT rate.

As regular physical activity plays an important role in preventing lifestyle-related diseases and supporting mental and physical well-being, higher VAT rates may reduce affordability and participation. We would therefore like to ask the Commission: 1.

Does it consider it important that access to sport and fitness services remains affordable in the light of their preventive benefits for public health, and will the Commission assess whether the current VAT framework under Directive 2006/112/EC2 adequately supports public health objectives, and whether reduced or minimum VAT rates for such services should be considered?

Will the forthcoming EU strategy on cardiovascular disease, or other initiatives on noncommunicable diseases, examine the affordability of physical activity services having preventive benefits, including their VAT treatment, and, if not, how and when does the Commission intend to address this issue?
What assessments has the Commission made, or can it make, regarding the public health and economic impacts of applying the full VAT rate?

Judgment of the Court of Justice of 22 September 2022, The Escape Center BVBA v Belgische Staat, C330/21, ECLI:EU:C:2022:719. OJ L 347, 11.12.2006, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2006/112/oj.
answer: 1. The Commission acknowledges the role of physical activity in the prevention of non-communicable diseases and encourages Member States to facilitate access to participation in sport activities, including for socioeconomically disadvantaged groups. When approving the reform to the value-added tax (VAT) rates system in 2022 (1), the Council of the EU addressed the issue raised by the Honourable Members.

Member States unanimously agreed on a new wording allowing them to apply a reduced VAT rate to the use of sporting facilities (2), now covering the supply of sports or physical exercise classes, including live-streamed ones.

The Commission believes that the new rules adequately support the efforts of Member States to protect and improve the health of their citizens by providing them with sufficient flexibility to apply a reduced VAT rate for these areas. 2. The Commission supports Member States to address non-communicable diseases and their risk factors through the ‘Healthier Together’ initiative (3).

With funding of EUR 76 million from the EU4Health programme, Member States are working together to address health determinants (4), such as by supporting local authorities to increase access to physical activity facilities. The Safe Hearts Plan (5) will continue to support Member States through targeted actions, to promote physical activity and raise awareness. 3.

Bearing in mind the responsibilities of the Member States in the area of VAT as well as for public health, the Commission has not conducted an assessment of the economic impact of the choices Member States made when applying the VAT Directive combined with the choices made in the area of public health.
